claim: HBV infection is a major global health problem, with chronic infection leading to liver complications and high death toll.
source: The hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a major global health problem, with chronic infection leading to liver complications and high death toll.
evidence: This is a general statement about HBV's public health impact, drawing from established scientific consensus.

claim: Current treatments such as nucleos(t)ide analogs and interferon-α effectively suppress viral replication but rarely cure the infection.
source: Current treatments, such as nucleos(t)ide analogs and interferon-α, effectively suppress viral replication but rarely cure the infection.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about current HBV treatment outcomes.

claim: A geranyl dimer binds to the central hydrophobic pocket of HBc-dimers with micromolar affinity.
source: We synthesized a geranyl dimer that binds to the central pocket with micromolar affinity
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC experimental data presented in the manuscript showing KD values.

claim: Dimeric peptides bind the spike-tip pocket with sub-micromolar affinity.
source: dimeric peptides that bind the spike-tip pocket with sub-micromolar affinity
evidence: This is supported by ITC measurements showing KD values in the sub-micromolar range for P1 dimers.

claim: Cryo-electron microscopy confirmed the binding of peptide dimers to the capsid spike tips.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy further confirmed the binding of peptide dimers to the capsid spike tips and their capsid-aggregating properties.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data showing density at spike tips corresponding to bound peptides.

claim: Peptide dimers induce HBc aggregation in vitro.
source: Finally, we show that the peptide dimers induce HBc aggregation in vitro and in living cells.
evidence: This is supported by turbidity assays and cryo-EM observations showing aggregated capsids.

claim: Peptide dimers induce HBc aggregation in living cells.
source: Finally, we show that the peptide dimers induce HBc aggregation in vitro and in living cells.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data showing HBc aggregates in transfected HEK293 cells treated with P1dC.

claim: Among children, the recovery rate from HBV infection is approximately 50%.
source: In childhood and infancy, the virus is particularly dangerous as the recovery rate among children is approximately 50%, while among infants infected through perinatal transmission, only 10% will naturally recover, the remainder will develop chronic infection (Thomas, 2019; Block et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Thomas, 2019 and Block et al., 2021.

claim: Among infants infected through perinatal transmission, only 10% will naturally recover from HBV infection.
source: In childhood and infancy, the virus is particularly dangerous as the recovery rate among children is approximately 50%, while among infants infected through perinatal transmission, only 10% will naturally recover, the remainder will develop chronic infection (Thomas, 2019; Block et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Thomas, 2019 and Block et al., 2021.

claim: There are about 300 million chronic HBV carriers globally.
source: With about 300 million chronic carriers and over 800,000 hepatitis-related yearly deaths, chronic hepatitis B is a global health problem (Block et al., 2021; World Health Organisation, 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Block et al., 2021 and World Health Organisation, 2022.

claim: There are over 800,000 hepatitis-related yearly deaths.
source: With about 300 million chronic carriers and over 800,000 hepatitis-related yearly deaths, chronic hepatitis B is a global health problem (Block et al., 2021; World Health Organisation, 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Block et al., 2021 and World Health Organisation, 2022.

claim: Nucleos(t)ide analogs compete for binding with natural nucleotide substrates, inhibiting viral protein P.
source: NAs compete for binding with the natural nucleotide substrates, inhibiting the viral protein P in charge of the reverse transcription of the viral pre-genomic RNA (pgRNA) into HBV DNA (Menéndez-Arias et al., 2014)
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citation to Menéndez-Arias et al., 2014.

claim: IFN-α activates genes with diverse antiviral functions to target various steps of viral replication.
source: IFN-α serves as both an immunomodulator and immunostimulant, activating genes with diverse antiviral functions to target various steps of viral replication. Additionally, it indirectly suppresses HBV infection by modifying cell-mediated immunity (Liang et al., 2015).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citation to Liang et al., 2015.

claim: Current HBV treatments effectively suppress viral replication and reduce liver inflammation, fibrosis, and the risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: Present treatments effectively suppress HBV replication, reduce liver inflammation, fibrosis, and the risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about the efficacy of current HBV treatments.

claim: IFN-α treatment is associated with significant adverse effects.
source: but IFN-α treatment is associated with significant adverse effects
evidence: This is established knowledge about IFN-α side effects.

claim: NAs typically require long-term oral administration, often lifelong.
source: NAs typically require long-term oral administration, often lifelong, as treatment discontinuation often results in viral rebound and disease recurrence in many patients.
evidence: This reflects established clinical knowledge about NA treatment duration.

claim: Treatment discontinuation of NAs often results in viral rebound and disease recurrence.
source: NAs typically require long-term oral administration, often lifelong, as treatment discontinuation often results in viral rebound and disease recurrence in many patients.
evidence: This reflects established clinical knowledge about NA treatment outcomes.

claim: A clinical cure of HBV is seldom achieved with current therapies.
source: While current therapies manage the disease, a clinical cure is seldom achieved, and the risk of HCC, although reduced, remains (Jeng et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jeng et al., 2023.

claim: Entry inhibitors disrupt HBV entry into hepatocytes by blocking binding to the NTCP receptor.
source: entry inhibitors that disrupt HBV entry into hepatocytes by blocking the binding to the sodium/taurocholate co-transporting polypeptide (NTCP) receptor (Yan et al., 2012).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citation to Yan et al., 2012.

claim: CAMs target the hepatitis B core protein (HBc) that participates in multiple essential steps of the HBV life cycle.
source: Finally, the capsid assembly modulators (CAMs) target the hepatitis B core protein (HBc) that participates in multiple essential steps of the HBV life cycle (Jeng et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jeng et al., 2023.

claim: Among direct acting antivirals in preclinical or clinical studies, a third are CAMs.
source: Among the direct acting antivirals that are in preclinical or clinical studies, a third are CAMs (Hepatitis B Foundation, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hepatitis B Foundation, 2023.

claim: The HBV capsid is composed of 120 units of HBc dimers, assembling into a T = 4 icosahedron.
source: The capsid is composed of 120 units of HBc dimers, assembling into a T = 4 icosahedron. Within this structure, 60 asymmetric units are formed by four HBc monomers each, designated as A, B, C, and D, or AB dimers and CD dimers (Crowther et al., 1994).
evidence: This structural information is supported by citation to Crowther et al., 1994.

claim: CAMs strengthen the association energy between HBc-dimer subunits, thereby promoting capsid assembly.
source: CAMs target the hydrophobic pocket at the HBc dimer–dimer interface, upon binding they strengthen the association energy between HBc-dimer subunits, thereby promoting capsid assembly, rather than inhibiting it (Venkatakrishnan et al., 2016; Stray et al., 2005).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citations to Venkatakrishnan et al., 2016 and Stray et al., 2005.

claim: CAMs can result in the formation of abnormal or empty capsids, sometimes accompanied by aggregation of core proteins.
source: As a result, abnormal or empty capsids may form, sometimes accompanied by the aggregation of core proteins, consequently inhibiting HBV DNA replication.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of CAM action described in the context.

claim: CAMs can disrupt the disassembly of incoming virions and the intracellular recycling of capsids.
source: Additionally, CAMs can disrupt the disassembly of incoming virions and the intracellular recycling of capsids, thereby impeding the establishment and replenishment of cccDNA (Jeng et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2021; Zoulim et al., 2022; Schlicksup and Zlotnick, 2020).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by multiple citations.

claim: TX100 targets a hydrophobic pocket formed at the base of the HBc spike, causing conformational alterations in the capsid structure.
source: Recently, a new potentially druggable site was discovered in the HBc dimer—a hydrophobic pocket formed at the base of the spike. This site was targeted by the detergent Triton X-100 (TX100), ultimately causing conformational alterations in the capsid structure (Lecoq et al., 2021; Makbul et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lecoq et al., 2021 and Makbul et al., 2021b.

claim: Peptides targeting the cleft on the spike tip reduced viral replication in a cell model.
source: Previous studies have shown that peptides targeting the cleft on the spike tip reduced viral replication in a cell model, likely by interfering with viral assembly through modulation of the HBc interaction with the surface antigen (Böttcher et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Böttcher et al., 1998.

claim: Myristylation of the large hepatitis B virus surface protein (L-HBs) is essential for HBV infectivity.
source: Hydrophobic post-translational modifications, such as myristylation of the large hepatitis B virus surface protein (L-HBs), are essential for HBV infectivity and play a role in mediating viral assembly (Gripon et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gripon et al., 1995.

claim: Farnesylation is involved in the envelopment of hepatitis D virus (HDV).
source: Additionally, farnesylation, another hydrophobic post-translational modification, is involved in the envelopment of hepatitis D virus (HDV) (Koh et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koh et al., 2015.

claim: TX100 was identified as a ligand of a distinct hydrophobic pocket in the center of HBc-dimers.
source: Recently, TX100, a nonionic surfactant sharing a similar hydrocarbon binding motif as the natural HBV post-translational modifications, was identified as a ligand of a distinct hydrophobic pocket in the center of HBc-dimers (Lecoq et al., 2021; Makbul et al., 2021b; Roseman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lecoq et al., 2021, Makbul et al., 2021b, and Roseman et al., 2005.

claim: Amino acids K96 and 129-PPAY-132 are involved in the secretion of enveloped virions from the cell.
source: Several of the pocket forming amino acids, such as K96 and 129-PPAY-132 (Rost et al., 2006) and the natural occurring point mutations HBcP5T, L60V, F97L, and P130T (; Le Pogam et al., 2000; Yuan and Shih, 2000; Yuan et al., 1999a; Ehata et al., 1992) are involved in the secretion of enveloped virions from the cell.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rost et al., 2006.

claim: Natural occurring point mutations HBcP5T, L60V, F97L, and P130T are involved in the secretion of enveloped virions from the cell.
source: Several of the pocket forming amino acids, such as K96 and 129-PPAY-132 (Rost et al., 2006) and the natural occurring point mutations HBcP5T, L60V, F97L, and P130T (; Le Pogam et al., 2000; Yuan and Shih, 2000; Yuan et al., 1999a; Ehata et al., 1992) are involved in the secretion of enveloped virions from the cell.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Le Pogam et al., 2000, Yuan and Shih, 2000, Yuan et al., 1999a, and Ehata et al., 1992.

claim: DM binds to HBc capsids with a KD of 133 ± 38 µM.
source: The isothermal calorimetric titration (ITC) of HBc capsids with DM (1) resolved micromolar affinity (KD = 133 ± 38 µM) to all four hydrophobic pockets of HBc capsids' asymmetric unit (N = 1.05 ± 0.1) (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Geraniol binds to HBc with a KD of 94 ± 8 µM.
source: ITC of geraniol with HBc showed a slightly enhanced micromolar affinity (KD = 94 ± 8 µM) (Figure 2A and B, Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and a stoichiometry of N = 1.01 ± 0.04
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Geraniol occupies all four hydrophobic pockets within the asymmetric unit of HBc capsids.
source: This experiment resolved an additional density for geraniol in all four hydrophobic pockets within the asymmetric unit of HBc capsids (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data showing density in all four pockets.

claim: Geraniol binding involves HBV residues P5, L60, K96, and F97.
source: This experiment resolved an additional density for geraniol in all four hydrophobic pockets within the asymmetric unit of HBc capsids (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), confirming the thermodynamic binding data and further defining the underlying molecular interactions of the involved HBV residues P5, L60, K96, and F97.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural analysis showing molecular interactions.

claim: The geranyl dimer has an affinity of 63 ± 8 µM to HBc capsids.
source: The analysis suggested that the dimer engages with both HBc binding sites simultaneously, resulting, however, only in a moderately enhanced micromolar affinity of 63 ± 8 µM (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data.

claim: Phage display-derived peptides MHRSLLGRMKGA (P1), GSLLGRMKGA (P2), and SLLGRM bind to wild-type HBc with KDs of 26, 68, and 130 µM, respectively.
source: Recently, we have shown that these peptides MHRSLLGRMKGA (P1), GSLLGRMKGA (P2), and the core binding motif SLLGRM bind to wild-type (wt) and mutant HBc variants (P5T, L60V and F97L) with intermediate micromolar KDs of 26, 68, and 130 µM, respectively (Makbul et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Makbul et al., 2021a.

claim: The SLLGRM-dimer has a KD of 4.9 ± 0.7 µM to HBc.
source: With a KD value of 4.9 ± 0.7 µM, the SLLGRM-dimer (4) has the lowest affinity to HBc
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data.

claim: The P2-dimer has a KD of 1.9 ± 0.4 µM to HBc.
source: followed by the P2-dimer (5) (KD = 1.9 ± 0.4 µM).
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data.

claim: The P1-dimers display sub-micromolar affinities of 312 nM and 420 nM to HBc.
source: Finally, the P1-dimers (6) and (7) displayed sub-micromolar affinities of 312 nM and 420 nM.
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data.

claim: P1-, P2-, and SLLGRM-dimers show 83-, 36-, and 27-fold increased affinities compared to their monomeric counterparts.
source: Thus, P1-, P2-, and SLLGRM-dimers show 83-, 36-, and 27-fold increased affinities compared to their monomeric counterparts.
evidence: This is calculated from the comparison of dimer and monomer KD values presented in the manuscript.

claim: The minimal sequence SLLGRM is the major mediator of HBc binding.
source: The analysis recapitulated our earlier resolved sequence requirement for HBc binding and substantiated that the minimal sequence SLLGRM is the major mediator of HBc binding.
evidence: This is supported by peptide microarray binding assay data showing reduced binding when SLLGRM is varied.

claim: The additional N-terminal residues in P1 sequence are neither conserved nor critically required for binding despite their importance in inducing HBc aggregation.
source: Importantly, it further indicates that the additional N-terminal residues in P1 sequence are neither conserved nor critically required for binding despite their importance in inducing HBc aggregation.
evidence: This is inferred from the peptide microarray data and turbidity assay results.

claim: P1dC has an affinity of 420 ± 38 nM to HBc.
source: The ITC confirmed that P1dC has an affinity of 420 ± 38 nM, comparable to P1-dimer
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data.

claim: The scrambled peptide scrP1dC did not display binding to HBc.
source: while the scrambled peptide did not display binding to HBc (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by ITC experimental data showing no heat change.

claim: P1dC induces aggregates of HBc in transfected HEK293 cells at 10 µM concentration.
source: Yet, upon administration of 10 µM of P1dC (7), we observed aggregates of HBc (in the form of large bright spots) within the cells (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy images showing bright aggregates in treated cells.

claim: The scrambled dimer scrP1dC at 10 µM did not induce HBc aggregation in cells.
source: At a concentration of 10 µM, the scrambled dimer scrP1dC did not induce aggregation and the distribution of HBc remained largely homogenous.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy images showing diffuse HBc distribution.

claim: P1dC induces large protein aggregates with multimicron diameter when incubated with CLPs.
source: The effect of peptide dimers on CLPs was already seen on the microscale cryo-EM images (Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2), with P1dC inducing large protein aggregates with multimicron diameter.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM micrographs showing large dark aggregates.

claim: SLLGRM-dimer induces visible aggregation of CLPs with smaller aggregate size than P1dC.
source: The less potent SLLGRM-dimer also induced visible aggregation, although with smaller aggregate size
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM micrographs showing aggregates.

claim: Geraniol-treated CLP samples showed minimal aggregation with the smallest observed aggregate sizes.
source: while geraniol-treated samples showed minimal aggregation, and the smallest observed aggregate sizes.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM micrographs showing few small aggregates.

claim: The densities corresponding to bound peptide-dimers have volumes that can accommodate a peptide chain of approximately six amino acid residues.
source: The densities corresponding to bound peptide-dimers in both EM-reconstructions have volumes, which can accommodate a peptide chain of approximately six amino acid residues (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the EM density volumes.

claim: The SLLGRM-dimer binds to both the A/B-dimer and the C/D-dimer of HBc capsids.
source: Interestingly, the SLLGRM-dimer binds the A/B-dimer as well as the C/D-dimer, in contrast to the monomeric SLLGRM, which binds only to the tip of the C/D-dimer (Makbul et al., 2021a; Figure 5)
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data and comparison with previous work.

claim: Monomeric SLLGRM binds only to the tip of the C/D-dimer.
source: Interestingly, the SLLGRM-dimer binds the A/B-dimer as well as the C/D-dimer, in contrast to the monomeric SLLGRM, which binds only to the tip of the C/D-dimer (Makbul et al., 2021a; Figure 5)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Makbul et al., 2021a.

claim: Point mutations within HBc can significantly affect HBV infectivity through disruptions in HBc interactions.
source: Earlier works demonstrated that point mutations within the HBc can significantly affect HBV infectivity, particularly through disruptions in HBc interactions (Yuan et al., 1999b; Bruss, 2007; Ponsel and Bruss, 2003; Koschel et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yuan et al., 1999b, Bruss, 2007, Ponsel and Bruss, 2003, and Koschel et al., 1999.

claim: TX100 binding within the hydrophobic pocket influences the spike tips by flipping Phe97.
source: However, TX100 binding within the hydrophobic pocket influences the spike tips by flipping Phe97, whereas geraniols bound within the same pocket do not induce this change, indicating that this interaction is ligand-specific.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of structural data for TX100 and geraniol binding.

claim: Geraniols bound within the hydrophobic pocket do not induce flipping of Phe97.
source: However, TX100 binding within the hydrophobic pocket influences the spike tips by flipping Phe97, whereas geraniols bound within the same pocket do not induce this change, indicating that this interaction is ligand-specific.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data showing no conformational change in Phe97.

claim: P2 peptide binding to the capsid spikes increases flexibility.
source: HBV capsid structural analysis showed that P2 peptide binding to the capsid spikes increases flexibility (Makbul et al., 2021a)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Makbul et al., 2021a.

claim: P2 peptide binding exerts minimal impact on the hydrophobic pocket beneath the spike.
source: HBV capsid structural analysis showed that P2 peptide binding to the capsid spikes increases flexibility (Makbul et al., 2021a) while exerting a minimal impact on the hydrophobic pocket beneath.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis cited in Makbul et al., 2021a.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations reveal significant flexibility of HBV capsids.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations revealed significant flexibility of the HBV capsids and suggested that structural asymmetry may affect ligand binding (Pavlova et al., 2018; Perilla et al., 2016; Pavlova et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pavlova et al., 2018, Perilla et al., 2016, and Pavlova et al., 2022.

claim: Structural asymmetry in HBV capsids may affect ligand binding.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations revealed significant flexibility of the HBV capsids and suggested that structural asymmetry may affect ligand binding (Pavlova et al., 2018; Perilla et al., 2016; Pavlova et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a suggestion from molecular dynamics simulations cited.

claim: The major capsid type formed by recombinant HBc in E. coli is composed of 240 subunits (T = 4) and represents approximately 95% of CLPs.
source: The major capsid type (ca. 95%) was formed by 240 subunits (Triangulation: T = 4).
evidence: This is based on characterization of purified CLPs used in the study.

claim: Binding of SLLGRM-dimer or P1dC splays the helices at the tips of spikes apart.
source: Binding of an (4) or of (7) splays the helices at the tips apart similar as previously reported for binding of a P2-monomer (Makbul et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data and comparison with previous work.

claim: Geraniol binds at the center of the spikes and does not change the conformation at the tips of the spikes.
source: Geraniol binds at the center of the spikes and does not change the conformation at the tips of the spikes.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data showing no conformational change at spike tips.

claim: P1 dimer induces turbidity of HBc solution at 1:10 equivalents of HBc.
source: We found that P1 dimer induces turbidity of a HBc solution already at 1:10 equivalents of HBc
evidence: This is supported by turbidity assay data.

claim: P2 dimer is slightly less potent than P1 dimer at inducing turbidity.
source: whereas the P2 dimer was slightly less potent
evidence: This is supported by turbidity assay data.

claim: SLLGRM dimer requires significantly higher concentration ratios relative to HBc to induce turbidity compared to P1 and P2 dimers.
source: and the SLLGRM dimer did not induce turbidity at the same conditions and further required significantly higher concentrations ratio relative to HBc (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by turbidity assay data.

claim: Capsids are attractive targets for HBV therapy due to the absence of human homologues for HBc.
source: Capsids are attractive targets due to the absence of human homologues for HBc and their involvement in crucial stages of the HBV life cycle
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about why capsids are good drug targets.

claim: HBc is involved in nuclear entry, encapsulation of pgRNA and polymerase, optional nuclear recycling to replenish the cccDNA pool, and eventual coating and secretion from infected cells.
source: Capsids are attractive targets due to the absence of human homologues for HBc and their involvement in crucial stages of the HBV life cycle, including nuclear entry, encapsulation of the pgRNA and polymerase, optional nuclear recycling to replenish the covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) pool, and eventual coating and secretion from infected cells (Jeng et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jeng et al., 2023 and Kim et al., 2021.

claim: Vaccinations are ineffective for individuals who are already infected with HBV.
source: Furthermore, vaccinations are ineffective for individuals who are already infected (Dienstag et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dienstag et al., 1982.
